MHHS2401 · Week 6 · Muscles of the gluteal region & posterior thigh

Gluteal Region & Posterior Thigh the buttock, the hamstrings, and the great nerve between them

One lecture built the way you dissect the region: landmarks first, then the muscles peeled superficial-to-deep, then the nerves and vessels threading past piriformis, the bones they pull on, and finally the hamstrings and the diamond behind the knee — decoded from Dr Mirjana Strkalj's L12 using its own figures.

§0Part A · orientation

Orientation — how the region is built

Two regions, one great nerve, and a deliberate order: landmarks → muscles → nerves → bones → hamstrings.

This lecture crosses the back of the pelvis and thigh. The gluteal region (the buttock) sits behind the pelvis, between the iliac crest and the gluteal fold. The posterior thigh is the flexor compartment behind the femur, holding the hamstrings. Running through both is the sciatic nerve — the single largest nerve in the body — which is why so much of this region is organised around where the nerve is and how to avoid it.

The deck sets three explicit learning outcomes, and this guide is built to answer them in a purposeful order:

  • LO1 — identify the gluteal muscles and explain their actions on the hip (§1–§3).
  • LO2 — identify the bony features of the femoral shaft, distal femur, and proximal tibia and fibula (§6).
  • LO3 — identify the posterior-thigh (hamstring) muscles and explain their actions at the hip and knee (§7–§8).
Reasoning · why nerves and foramina come before injections

You cannot understand the "safe quadrant" for a gluteal injection (§5), why piriformis syndrome exists (§4), or why the short head of biceps has its own nerve (§7) until you know where the sciatic nerve runs and which openings it uses. So we lay down the landmarks (§1), peel the muscles superficial→deep (§2–§3), and only then trace the vessels and nerve (§4) — each part is the foundation the next stands on.

Memory hook · the two-nerve rule of the buttock

Superior gluteal nerve = medius, minimus, TFL (the abductors). Inferior gluteal nerve = gluteus maximus alone (the extensor). Everything posterior-thigh = sciatic. Fix these three and half the region's questions answer themselves.

Clinical / real-world

The recurring clinical thread of this lecture is nerve injury: gluteus medius weakness (Trendelenburg gait), sciatic injury from a misplaced injection, and common fibular injury at the fibular neck (foot-drop). Read every muscle asking "what nerve, and what happens if it fails?"

§1Part B · surface & bony landmarks

The gluteal region — landmarks you can feel

Before muscles: the borders, folds and palpable bony points that frame the buttock.

The gluteal region lies posterior to the pelvis, bounded above by the iliac crest and below by the gluteal sulcus (the buttock fold). Crucially, that fold is not the lower edge of the muscle — it is formed by the fat pad lying over the inferior border of gluteus maximus. The two buttocks are separated in the midline by the intergluteal (natal) cleft. As Plate 1.1 shows, the same surface hides a set of bony points you can palpate to orient every deeper structure.

Label Key — landmarks of the gluteal region
Highest level of iliac crest
Top border of the region; the transverse supracristal plane through it crosses the L4 spinous process — the safe landmark for a lumbar puncture.
Intergluteal (natal) cleft
Midline groove separating the buttocks; overlies the sacrum and coccyx.
Sacrum & coccyx
Origin of much of gluteus maximus; the coccyx is palpable at the top of the cleft.
PSIS (posterior superior iliac spine)
Marked by a skin dimple; a reliable bony landmark and the medial edge of the safe injection zone (§5).
Gluteal fold / sulcus
The buttock crease, formed by the fat pad over gluteus maximus's inferior border — marks the lower limit of the region, not the muscle edge.
Site of greater trochanter
Lateral bony prominence of the femur; insertion point for medius/minimus and the deep rotators, and a key injection landmark.
Site of ischial tuberosity
The "sitting bone"; common origin of the hamstrings and of several deep rotators.
Nélaton's line
A line from the ASIS to the ischial tuberosity; the tip of the greater trochanter normally lies on it — displacement suggests a hip fracture or dislocation.
Site of tensor fasciae latae
Anterolateral to the region; tenses the iliotibial tract (§2).
Reasoning · why the fold is fat, not muscle

Gluteus maximus fibres run obliquely downward and laterally to the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity — its lower border cuts diagonally across the buttock, not horizontally. The visible horizontal fold is instead where a subcutaneous fat pad creases as the buttock meets the thigh. This is why the fold stays put even when the muscle contracts, and why it is a surface marker rather than a muscular one.

Memory hook · "crest to L4"

The supracristal plane (top of the iliac crests) → L4 spinous process. Palpate both crests, draw the line between them, and you are at L4 — one level above where the spinal cord ends, so it is safe for a lumbar puncture.

Clinical / real-world

Nélaton's line is a bedside test: if the tip of the greater trochanter rises above the ASIS–ischial-tuberosity line, the femur has shortened or ridden up — as in a femoral neck fracture or posterior hip dislocation.

§2Part B · superficial muscle group

Superficial glutei — maximus, medius, minimus & TFL

One big extensor, two abductors, and the tensor that guards the knee.

Peel the skin and fat and you meet the superficial group: three glutei (maximus, medius, minimus) plus tensor fasciae latae (TFL). Functionally they split cleanly — gluteus maximus is the extensor, while medius, minimus and TFL are the abductors and medial rotators. Plate 2.1 shows maximus and TFL feeding into the iliotibial tract; Plate 2.2 shows what happens when medius fails.

§2.1Gluteus maximus — the powerhouse extensor

The largest and most superficial gluteal muscle. It has a broad origin: posterior to the posterior gluteal line of the ilium, the dorsal surface of the sacrum and coccyx, and the sacrotuberous ligament. It inserts into the iliotibial tract (the majority of its fibres) and the gluteal tuberosity of the femur (its deep distal fibres). As Plate 2.1(B) shows, this split insertion is why the muscle both stabilises the knee (via the tract) and extends the hip (via the femur).

  • Actions — extends the thigh, especially from a flexed position; assists rising from sitting; assists lateral rotation.
  • Nerve — inferior gluteal nerve.
Label Key — gluteus maximus & TFL
Gluteus maximus
The bulky extensor; fibres run down-and-out to the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity — powerful in climbing and standing from a squat.
Tensor fasciae latae (TFL)
Anterolateral muscle from the iliac crest/ASIS into the iliotibial tract; tenses the tract, helping stabilise the extended knee and abduct/medially rotate the hip.
Iliotibial tract
The thickened band of fascia lata down the lateral thigh; the shared tendon of maximus + TFL, inserting on the anterolateral (Gerdy's) tubercle of the tibia — braces the knee in stance.
Superficial ¾ of gluteus maximus
The larger part attaching to the iliotibial tract — the knee-bracing portion.
Deep distal ¼ of gluteus maximus
Attaches to the gluteal tuberosity of the femur — the true hip-extending portion.
Lateral intermuscular septum
Fascial wall over vastus lateralis; separates the anterior and posterior thigh compartments.
Anterolateral (Gerdy's) tubercle of tibia
Bony landmark where the iliotibial tract inserts — the tract's mechanical anchor at the knee.

§2.2Gluteus medius & minimus — the pelvic stabilisers

Both arise from a broad area of the external surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines, lying deep to maximus. Their insertions differ only in position on the greater trochanter — a favourite exam point:

  • Gluteus medius → lateral surface of the greater trochanter.
  • Gluteus minimus → anterior surface of the greater trochanter.
  • Main actions — abduct and medially rotate the thigh; and critically, keep the pelvis level when the opposite leg is raised.
  • Nerve — superior gluteal nerve.
Reasoning · how an "abductor" keeps you walking

In single-leg stance (every step), the unsupported side of the pelvis wants to drop under gravity. The stance-limb gluteus medius/minimus contract to pull the pelvis down toward their own (fixed) femur, which holds the opposite side level. So their headline job in walking is not swinging the leg out — it is a reverse-origin action stabilising the pelvis on the planted limb.

Label Key — the Trendelenburg sign
Normal (level pelvis)
Standing on one leg, the stance-side gluteus medius holds the pelvis horizontal — the unsupported hip stays up.
Trendelenburg sign
When the stance-limb gluteus medius is weak, the pelvis drops on the side of the lifted leg — the side opposite the weak muscle.
Weak gluteus medius
The failing muscle is on the stance (weight-bearing) side, even though the visible drop is on the other side — the classic trap.
Memory hook · "sound side sags"

In a Trendelenburg sign, the sound (healthy) side sags. The pelvis drops on the side opposite the weak muscle, because that healthy side is the one being lifted. So a right pelvic drop = weak left gluteus medius (you are standing on the left/weak leg).

Clinical / real-world

A positive Trendelenburg sign points to gluteus medius dysfunction — from a superior gluteal nerve injury (e.g. a badly placed IM injection, §5), hip osteoarthritis, or a fractured femoral neck. The compensatory "waddling" (Trendelenburg) gait leans the trunk over the stance limb to shift the centre of gravity and spare the failing abductors.

§2.3Tensor fasciae latae

TFL runs from the iliac crest/ASIS into the iliotibial tract. Sharing that tract with gluteus maximus, it tenses the tract, helping stabilise the extended knee and contributing to abduction and medial rotation of the hip. It is supplied, like medius/minimus, by the superior gluteal nerve — grouping it with the abductors both anatomically and neurologically.

Superficial gluteal group — origin, insertion, action, nerve
MuscleOriginInsertionMain actionNerve
Gluteus maximusBehind posterior gluteal line; dorsal sacrum & coccyx; sacrotuberous ligamentIliotibial tract & gluteal tuberosityExtends thigh (esp. from flexed); lateral rotation; rising from sittingInferior gluteal
Gluteus mediusExternal ilium, between ant. & post. gluteal linesLateral surface of greater trochanterAbduct & medially rotate thigh; level pelvis in stanceSuperior gluteal
Gluteus minimusExternal ilium, between ant. & post. gluteal linesAnterior surface of greater trochanterAbduct & medially rotate thigh; level pelvis in stanceSuperior gluteal
Tensor fasciae lataeIliac crest / ASISIliotibial tractTenses tract; stabilises extended knee; abduct/medially rotate hipSuperior gluteal
§3Part B · deep muscle group

Deep lateral rotators of the hip

Six short muscles fanning from the pelvis to the greater trochanter — the buttock's steering wheel.

Lift the glutei and you reach the deep group: piriformis, obturator internus, superior and inferior gemelli, and quadratus femoris (obturator externus is deeper still). Running roughly horizontally from pelvis to greater trochanter, they are the lateral (external) rotators of the thigh. Plate 3.1 shows them fanning out; Plate 3.2 names their bony relations. Learn piriformis first — it is the landmark against which every vessel and nerve in §4 is described.

Label Key — the deep rotators
Piriformis muscle
From the anterior sacrum to the superior border of the greater trochanter; the key landmark dividing the greater sciatic foramen into "above" and "below" (§4).
Greater sciatic foramen above piriformis
Exit for the superior gluteal nerve and vessels.
Greater sciatic foramen below piriformis
Exit for the inferior gluteal vessels/nerve, sciatic nerve and pudendal nerve — the crowded, clinically dangerous gap.
Obturator internus
From the obturator membrane inside the pelvis; its tendon hooks through the lesser sciatic foramen to the medial greater trochanter — lateral rotator.
Gemellus superior
Small slip from the ischial spine blending with the obturator internus tendon; supplied by the nerve to obturator internus.
Gemellus inferior
Small slip from the ischial tuberosity blending with the obturator internus tendon; supplied by the nerve to quadratus femoris.
Quadratus femoris
Flat quadrilateral muscle from the ischial tuberosity to the quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest — a pure lateral rotator.
Gluteus medius / minimus (reflected)
Shown cut to expose the deep group beneath.
Ischial tuberosity / Femur / Greater trochanter
The bony origins (ischium) and common insertion target (greater trochanter) of the deep group.

Each muscle's exact origin, insertion, nerve and action are worth committing to memory; the deck lists them individually and they share a near-identical action:

Deep lateral rotators — origin, insertion, innervation, action
MuscleOriginInsertionInnervationAction
PiriformisAnterior surface of sacrumSuperior border of greater trochanterBranches from L5, S1, S2Laterally rotate extended thigh; abduct flexed thigh
Obturator internusObturator membrane & surrounding boneMedial surface of greater trochanterNerve to obturator internusLaterally rotate extended thigh; abduct flexed thigh
Gemellus superiorIschial spineMedial surface of greater trochanterNerve to obturator internusLaterally rotate extended thigh; abduct flexed thigh
Gemellus inferiorSuperior aspect of ischial tuberosityMedial surface of greater trochanterNerve to quadratus femorisLaterally rotate extended thigh; abduct flexed thigh
Quadratus femorisLateral aspect of ischial tuberosityQuadrate tubercle on intertrochanteric crestNerve to quadratus femorisLaterally rotate the thigh

§3.1Bony relations of the deep group

Plate 3.2 strips the muscles to show the ligaments and bone they cross. Note the obturator internus tendon emerging through the lesser sciatic foramen, flanked by the gemelli — together the three are the triceps coxae. The tendon of piriformis reaches the greater trochanter, and the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments convert the sciatic notches into the greater and lesser foramina.

Label Key — foramina, ligaments & the triceps coxae
Greater sciatic foramen
The main opening from pelvis to buttock; piriformis passes through it and subdivides it.
Sacrospinous ligament
Runs from sacrum to ischial spine; its lower border separates the greater from the lesser sciatic foramen.
Sacrotuberous ligament
From sacrum to ischial tuberosity; converts the lesser sciatic notch into the lesser sciatic foramen and gives origin to gluteus maximus.
Tendon of piriformis
Attaches to the greater trochanter; the reference point for the sciatic nerve's exit.
Trochanteric fossa
Pit on the medial greater trochanter receiving obturator externus.
Superior gemellus / Obturator internus / Inferior gemellus
The triceps coxae — insert together on the medial greater trochanter via the obturator internus tendon.
Obturator internus inside pelvis / through lesser sciatic foramen
Shows the muscle turning ~90° around the ischium as it leaves the pelvis — a bony pulley.
Obturator externus
Deepest lateral rotator, crossing the back of the hip joint to the trochanteric fossa.
Ischial tuberosity / Lesser trochanter / Greater trochanter
Bony origins and insertions of the deep group.
Reasoning · why they are all lateral rotators

Every muscle here runs roughly horizontally from a posterior/medial pelvic origin to the greater trochanter, which sits lateral to the hip's vertical axis. Pulling the trochanter backward and medially spins the femur outward — lateral rotation. Their more horizontal fibres also mean that, once the hip is flexed (changing their line of pull), several instead abduct — which is exactly what the deck lists for piriformis, obturator internus and the gemelli.

Memory hook · "P-GO-GO-Q" from top to bottom

Top → bottom on the pelvis: Piriformis · Gemellus superior · Obturator internus · Gemellus inferior · Quadratus femoris. The two gemelli sandwich obturator internus — hence "twins" (gemelli) either side of it.

Clinical / real-world

Because piriformis lies directly over the sciatic nerve's exit (§4), a tight or spasming piriformis can compress the nerve — piriformis syndrome — causing deep buttock pain radiating down the back of the thigh, mimicking a disc-related sciatica.

§4Part B · neurovasculature

Foramina, gluteal vessels & the sciatic nerve

Everything is described as "above" or "below" piriformis — and the great nerve usually runs below.

The gluteal region is a crossroads: structures pass between pelvis and limb through two openings. The greater sciatic foramen carries structures out to the buttock; the lesser sciatic foramen carries structures (and the obturator internus tendon) into the perineum. Piriformis threads through the greater foramen and divides it, so the whole neurovascular map reduces to a simple question: above piriformis or below? Plate 4.1 traces the vessels and nerve.

Label Key — gluteal neurovasculature
Superior gluteal artery & vein
Exit above piriformis with the superior gluteal nerve; supply medius, minimus and TFL.
Superficial branch (of superior gluteal a.)
Runs into gluteus maximus.
Deep branch (of superior gluteal a.)
Runs between medius and minimus to supply them and TFL.
Inferior gluteal artery & vein
Exit below piriformis; supply gluteus maximus and accompany the sciatic nerve.
Piriformis muscle
The dividing landmark; vessels/nerves are named by their position relative to it.
Lateral femoral circumflex artery
Anastomoses with the gluteal vessels around the hip — part of the trochanteric/cruciate anastomosis.
Medial femoral circumflex artery
The main blood supply to the femoral head; anastomoses with the gluteal system.
First perforating artery (from deep artery of thigh)
Contributes to the cruciate anastomosis at the back of the thigh, linking gluteal and femoral circulations.

The traffic through the greater sciatic foramen splits cleanly:

Structures leaving the greater sciatic foramen, relative to piriformis
Above piriformisBelow piriformis
Superior gluteal nerveInferior gluteal nerve
Superior gluteal artery & veinInferior gluteal artery & vein
 Sciatic nerve
 Pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels (then re-enter via lesser foramen)
 Nerve to obturator internus; posterior femoral cutaneous nerve

§4.1The sciatic nerve & its variants

The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body — really two nerves in one sheath: the tibial division and the common fibular (peroneal) division. It usually exits below piriformis, then descends deep to gluteus maximus into the posterior thigh, supplying every hamstring. But its relationship to piriformis varies, as Plate 4.2 shows — and those variants underlie piriformis syndrome.

Label Key — sciatic–piriformis variants
(A) Standard course
The whole sciatic nerve (tibial + common fibular) passes below piriformis — the commonest arrangement.
(B) Split around piriformis
The common fibular division pierces piriformis while the tibial part runs below — a common variant that predisposes to entrapment.
(C) Division above & below
The common fibular division passes above piriformis and the tibial part below — the muscle is caught between the two.
Tibial nerve
The larger, medial division; supplies the hamstrings and posterior leg.
Common fibular (peroneal) nerve
The lateral division; the part most often affected by variants and later vulnerable at the fibular neck.
Reasoning · why the sciatic nerve is "two nerves"

The tibial and common fibular divisions have different destinations — the tibial to the posterior leg and sole, the common fibular to the anterior/lateral leg and dorsum. They are only bundled together for convenience in the thigh. This is why a single variant (fibular part piercing piriformis) can knock out just one division, and why the two split at different levels in different people.

Clinical / real-world

Piriformis syndrome: in variant courses (Plate 4.2 B/C), contraction or spasm of piriformis compresses the sciatic (often the fibular) fibres, producing buttock pain radiating down the leg that worsens on sitting or hip rotation — a "sciatica" arising in the buttock rather than the spine.

Memory hook · "SUP above, everything else below"

Only the SUPerior gluteal nerve and vessels leave above piriformis. The inferior gluteal bundle, the sciatic, the pudendal — the whole crowd — leaves below. If in doubt, it's below.

§5Part B · clinical application

The safe quadrant for intramuscular injection

A whole slide devoted to not hitting the nerve you just learned to trace.

The buttock is a favourite site for intramuscular (IM) injection — plenty of muscle, easy access. But the sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal vessels lie in the lower medial region (they exit below piriformis, §4). So the rule is simple: inject into the upper outer (superolateral) quadrant, over gluteus medius, well away from the nerve. Plate 5.1 maps the safe area two ways.

Label Key — the safe injection zone
Safe area for injection
The upper outer (superolateral) quadrant, over gluteus medius — far from the sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal vessels.
Summit of iliac crest
Upper boundary of the safe zone.
Site of PSIS
Medial boundary; a vertical line from it marks the inner edge of the safe quadrant.
Superior gluteal nerve
Runs within the target muscle mass; a correctly placed, shallow injection spares it.
Site of greater trochanter
Inferolateral bony landmark bounding the zone.
Sciatic nerve
The structure to avoid — lies in the lower medial region beneath gluteus maximus.
Gluteus maximus / Biceps femoris
Marked to show the danger territory the needle must stay above and lateral to.
ASIS & iliac tubercle (lateral view, X)
In the ventrogluteal method, palm on the greater trochanter, index on the ASIS, middle finger to the iliac tubercle — inject into the V ("X").
Reasoning · why "upper outer" and not just "in the middle"

Divide the buttock into quadrants. The sciatic nerve leaves below piriformis and runs through the lower medial region toward the posterior thigh. Only the upper outer quadrant is guaranteed to sit over thick gluteus medius with no major nerve or vessel beneath — so it is the one square that is safe by geometry, not by luck.

Clinical / real-world

A needle placed too low and medial can strike the sciatic nerve → foot-drop and sensory loss, or the inferior gluteal vessels → haematoma. Injecting too far superomedially instead risks the superior gluteal nerve, weakening the abductors (Trendelenburg gait, §2). The modern ventrogluteal approach (Plate 5.1 B) is preferred precisely because the hand-landmark method keeps the needle over gluteus medius, clear of all of them.

Memory hook · "up and out, safe from doubt"

Upper outer quadrant = safe. Draw a cross over the buttock; the only quadrant with no big nerve under it is top-lateral.

§6Part C · bony features (LO2)

Bones — femur, tibia & fibula

The scaffold the muscles pull on: trochanters and tuberosities above, condyles and malleoli below.

Before the hamstrings, the deck steps back to the bones — because every action so far and to come is a pull on a named bony feature. We need the femur (shaft and distal end) and the proximal tibia and fibula. Read each feature as a muscle address: the gluteal tuberosity is where maximus lands, the greater trochanter where medius/minimus and the deep six land, the ischial-derived tibial sites where the hamstrings end.

§6.1The femur

Plate 6.1 shows the whole femur. Trace it top to bottom: head (with fovea) → neck (set at an angle of inclination) → greater and lesser trochanters → the intertrochanteric line (front) and crest with quadrate tubercle (back) → the shaft with its posterior linea aspera → the flared distal condyles.

Label Key — femur (muscle addresses in bold)
Head & fovea
Articular ball; the fovea anchors the ligament of the head (carrying a small artery).
Neck & angle of inclination
Angles the head medially onto the pelvis; a common fracture site in the elderly.
Greater trochanter
Lateral prominence — insertion of gluteus medius/minimus and the deep lateral rotators (§2–§3).
Lesser trochanter
Posteromedial; insertion of iliopsoas (hip flexor).
Intertrochanteric line (anterior) / crest (posterior)
Ridges joining the trochanters; the crest bears the quadrate tubercle for quadratus femoris.
Quadrate tubercle
On the intertrochanteric crest — insertion of quadratus femoris.
Trochanteric fossa
Medial pit on the greater trochanter — receives obturator externus.
Gluteal tuberosity
Roughened posterior ridge below the greater trochanter — insertion of the deep quarter of gluteus maximus.
Pectineal (spiral) line & linea aspera
Posterior ridges; the linea aspera's medial and lateral lips anchor adductors, vasti and the short head of biceps femoris.
Medial/lateral supracondylar lines
The splayed continuations of the linea aspera toward the condyles.
Medial & lateral condyles / epicondyles
The knee's articular surfaces and their overlying muscle/ligament bumps; the adductor tubercle sits above the medial condyle.
Intercondylar fossa & popliteal surface
Posterior notch (for the cruciate ligaments) and the flat area forming the floor of the popliteal fossa (§8).

§6.2Tibia & fibula

The leg has a weight-bearing tibia medially and a slender fibula laterally, joined along their interosseous borders by the interosseous membrane. Plate 6.2 shows the shafts (note the triangular tibial cross-section) and the fibula's head and lateral malleolus.

Label Key — tibia & fibula
Anterior / interosseous / medial borders (tibia)
The three edges of the triangular tibial shaft; the interosseous border faces the fibula.
Lateral / medial / posterior surfaces (tibia)
The three faces between those borders (see cross-section C).
Soleal line
Oblique ridge on the posterior tibia — origin of soleus (a floor-muscle of the popliteal fossa's exit).
Interosseous membrane
Fibrous sheet between the interosseous borders; transfers load from tibia to fibula and separates leg compartments.
Medial malleolus (tibia)
The inner ankle prominence — part of the ankle mortise.
Lateral malleolus (fibula)
The outer ankle prominence — the fibula's main functional role, stabilising the ankle.
Groove for tibialis posterior tendon
Behind the medial malleolus — routes the tendon into the foot.
Fibular groove on tibia / articular surfaces for talus
Where the fibula meets the tibia and the talus below — the ankle joint surfaces.

§6.3Proximal tibia — the hamstring landings

The proximal tibia is where two hamstrings (and pes anserinus muscles) end. Plate 6.3 shows the condyles, the intercondylar eminence, the tibial tuberosity, and — key for §7 — the medial site for sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus and the medial condyle for semimembranosus.

Label Key — proximal tibia
Tubercles of the intercondylar eminence
Central spikes between the condyles; anchor the cruciate ligaments and menisci.
Lateral & medial condyles
The tibial plateau's articular surfaces for the femoral condyles — the knee joint.
Tibial tuberosity
Anterior bump receiving the patellar ligament (quadriceps attachment).
Site of sartorius, gracilis & semitendinosus (pes anserinus)
Medial surface where these three tendons converge — semitendinosus lands here (§7).
Medial condyle
Also the insertion of semimembranosus.
Roughened & perforated area / groove
Sites for capsule and cruciate/meniscal attachments.
Soleal line (posterior)
Origin of soleus.
Articular facet for proximal head of fibula
Where the fibular head articulates — a small, minimally mobile joint.
Reasoning · why the fibula barely bears weight

The fibular head sits below and lateral to the tibial plateau, so it is not part of the knee joint and receives almost no downward load — force from the femur passes straight into the tibia. The fibula's real jobs are to anchor muscles (biceps femoris on its head; the leg's lateral compartment along its shaft) and to form the lateral malleolus that grips the talus at the ankle. Form follows function: a slender bone is enough for tension, not compression.

Memory hook · pes anserinus = "Say Grace before Tea"

The three tendons of the pes anserinus ("goose's foot") on the medial tibia, front to back: Sartorius, Gracilis, semiTendinosus — Say Grace before Tea. Only semitendinosus is a hamstring.

Clinical / real-world

The femoral neck and its angle of inclination make it a classic fragility-fracture site — and because the medial femoral circumflex artery (§4) supplies the head, a displaced neck fracture can cut off that blood supply and cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

§7Part D · posterior thigh (LO3)

Posterior thigh — the hamstrings

Three muscles from one bump, crossing two joints, driven by one nerve.

The posterior (flexor) compartment of the thigh holds the three hamstrings: semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris (long head), joined by the hamstring part of adductor magnus. They share a common origin at the ischial tuberosity (the short head of biceps is the exception) and, because they span both hip and knee, they do two jobs at once: extend the thigh at the hip and flex the leg at the knee. Their nerve is the tibial division of the sciatic nerve — except the short head of biceps. Plate 7.1 lays them out.

Label Key — the hamstrings
Biceps femoris — long head
From the ischial tuberosity; the lateral hamstring. With the short head it forms the tendon to the fibular head.
Biceps femoris — short head
From the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line — the only hamstring not from the ischial tuberosity, and the only one on the common fibular nerve.
Tendon of biceps femoris
The palpable lateral cord at the knee, inserting on the head of the fibula; forms the superolateral border of the popliteal fossa (§8).
Semitendinosus
Superficial medial hamstring with a long cord-like tendon to the pes anserinus (medial proximal tibia).
Semimembranosus
Deep medial hamstring (broad membranous origin) inserting on the medial tibial condyle.
Adductor magnus — hamstring part
The ischiocondylar portion; from the ischial tuberosity to the adductor tubercle — acts with the hamstrings to extend the hip and is (partly) sciatic-innervated.

The individual attachments, actions and nerves are the crux of LO3:

Hamstrings — origin, insertion, action, innervation
MuscleOriginInsertionActionInnervation
Biceps femoris (long head)Ischial tuberosityHead of fibula (common tendon)Flex & laterally rotate leg (knee); extend thigh (hip)Sciatic — tibial division
Biceps femoris (short head)Linea aspera & lateral supracondylar lineHead of fibula (common tendon)Flex & laterally rotate leg (knee)Sciatic — common fibular division
SemitendinosusIschial tuberosityMedial surface of proximal tibia (pes anserinus)Flex & medially rotate leg (knee); extend thigh (hip)Sciatic — tibial division
SemimembranosusIschial tuberosityMedial tibial condyleFlex & medially rotate leg (knee); extend thigh (hip)Sciatic — tibial division
Reasoning · why biceps rotates laterally and the "semis" rotate medially

Rotation of the flexed knee depends on which side a muscle's tendon crosses. Biceps femoris inserts laterally (fibular head), so pulling it spins the tibia outward — lateral rotation. Semitendinosus and semimembranosus insert medially (pes anserinus / medial condyle), so they spin the tibia inward — medial rotation. Insertion side dictates rotation direction — a rule you can reconstruct rather than memorise.

Memory hook · "the two SEMIs are medial; the BIceps is lateral"

Both SEMI muscles insert medially → medial rotators of the knee. BIceps inserts on the fibula (lateral) → lateral rotator. And only the SHort head of biceps is SHort on the ischial tuberosity (it starts on the femur) and runs on a different nerve.

Clinical / real-world

Hamstring strains ("pulled hamstring") typically tear near the ischial-tuberosity origin during explosive hip-extension/knee-flexion (sprinting). Because the hamstrings cross two joints, they are stretched maximally when the hip is flexed and the knee extended (as in a high kick) — the position of greatest injury risk (a consequence of the same two-joint anatomy that gives them active insufficiency).

§8Part D · the diamond behind the knee

Popliteal fossa & surface anatomy

Where the hamstrings part, the sciatic nerve splits, and everything becomes palpable.

As the hamstrings approach the knee they diverge, leaving a diamond-shaped hollow — the popliteal fossa. It is the gateway for nerves and vessels passing from thigh to leg, and it is where the sciatic nerve finishes splitting into its tibial and common fibular parts. Plate 8.1 shows its boundaries and contents; Plate 8.2 ties everything back to the living surface.

Label Key — popliteal fossa
Semimembranosus & semitendinosus (1, 2)
Form the superomedial boundary of the diamond.
Biceps femoris (6)
Forms the superolateral boundary; its tendon leads the common fibular nerve toward the fibular neck.
Gastrocnemius, medial & lateral heads (3, 5)
Form the two inferior boundaries; soleus (4) lies deep to them.
Bifurcation of sciatic nerve
The sciatic nerve divides here (or just above) into tibial and common fibular nerves.
Tibial nerve
Runs vertically through the fossa — the most superficial of the deep structures.
Common fibular (peroneal) nerve
Follows the biceps tendon laterally toward the fibular neck — vulnerable there.
Popliteal vein
Lies between the tibial nerve and the artery.
Popliteal artery
The deepest structure, against the joint capsule/femur — hence hard to compress and prone to injury in knee dislocation.
Small (short) saphenous vein
Pierces the fascia to drain into the popliteal vein.

The neurovascular contents stack in a memorable depth order — nerve, vein, artery from superficial to deep, as Plate 8.1(B) shows.

Memory hook · popliteal contents "NAVy, but reversed"

From superficial → deep: Nerves (tibial, then common fibular) → Vein → Artery. The artery is deepest (against the bone), which is why a popliteal pulse is hard to feel — press firmly with the knee slightly flexed.

§8.1Surface anatomy of the posterior thigh

Plate 8.2 projects all of this onto the skin. The sciatic nerve runs down the midline of the posterior thigh deep to gluteus maximus, splitting near the knee; the biceps tendon (lateral) and semitendinosus tendon (medial) are the palpable cords bounding the fossa; the iliotibial tract (§2) stands out over vastus lateralis.

Label Key — posterior thigh surface
Gluteus maximus
The buttock bulk under which the sciatic nerve descends.
Sciatic nerve (projection)
The dashed line down the midline of the thigh; splits into tibial and common fibular near the knee.
Iliotibial tract (over vastus lateralis)
The palpable lateral band — the shared tendon of gluteus maximus and TFL (§2).
Biceps femoris & biceps tendon
Lateral hamstring; its tendon is the palpable lateral border of the popliteal fossa.
Semitendinosus & its tendon / semimembranosus
Medial hamstrings; the semitendinosus tendon is the palpable medial fossa border.
Common fibular nerve
Traceable following the biceps tendon toward the fibular neck.
Tibial nerve / gastrocnemius heads
Descend through and below the fossa into the calf.
Adductor magnus & gracilis
Medial-thigh muscles bordering the region.
Reasoning · why the fossa is arranged nerve-outermost, artery-innermost

The popliteal artery is the direct continuation of the femoral artery passing through the adductor hiatus onto the back of the femur — so it necessarily lies deepest, against the bone. The vein accompanies it, and the nerves, arriving from the more superficial posterior compartment, lie most superficial. The depth order is a map of where each structure came from.

Clinical / real-world

The common fibular nerve at the fibular neck (Plate 8.2) is the most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb — a tight cast, crossed legs or a blow there causes foot-drop (loss of dorsiflexion and eversion). And because the popliteal artery is tethered deep in the fossa, a posterior knee dislocation can tear it — a limb-threatening emergency requiring urgent vascular assessment.

R Recall checklist — gluteal region & posterior thigh
  • Gluteal fold — formed by the fat pad over the inferior border of gluteus maximus; supracristal plane → L4.
  • Gluteus maximus — extends thigh (esp. from flexed); inserts iliotibial tract + gluteal tuberosity; inferior gluteal nerve.
  • Gluteus medius/minimus — abduct & medially rotate, level the pelvis in stance; greater trochanter (lateral vs anterior); superior gluteal nerve.
  • Trendelenburg sign — weak stance-side medius → pelvis drops on the opposite (lifted) side.
  • Deep six — piriformis, obturator internus, sup/inf gemelli, quadratus femoris = lateral rotators to the greater trochanter.
  • Piriformis rule — superior gluteal n./vessels exit above; sciatic, inferior gluteal, pudendal exit below.
  • Sciatic nerve — tibial + common fibular divisions; variant courses cause piriformis syndrome.
  • Safe injection — upper outer quadrant, over gluteus medius, away from the sciatic nerve.
  • Femur landmarks — greater trochanter (medius/minimus + deep six), gluteal tuberosity (maximus), quadrate tubercle (quadratus femoris).
  • Pes anserinus — sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus on the medial proximal tibia; semimembranosus on the medial condyle.
  • Hamstrings — common ischial-tuberosity origin (not biceps short head); extend hip + flex knee; tibial division (short head = common fibular).
  • Rotation rule — biceps = lateral rotator of the knee; the two "semis" = medial rotators.
  • Popliteal fossa — bounded by biceps, semimembranosus/semitendinosus, and gastrocnemius heads; contents nerve→vein→artery (superficial→deep).
  • Common fibular nerve at the fibular neck → foot-drop; popliteal artery deepest & vulnerable in knee dislocation.
